name: Kingdom of North Sudan (Bir Tawil)
pop: No permanent population; miners and tribes pass through
challenge: Never tested by a state in court or on the ground
recognition: None. A UN observer application was filed; no government recognised it
cost: Heaton estimated at least $2bn to start the project and sought up to $45m online
story: Bir Tawil is 2,060 square kilometres of desert between Egypt and Sudan. Britain drew a straight border along the 22nd parallel in 1899, then an administrative line in 1902 that followed how tribes used the land. Egypt uses the first line and Sudan the second, because each line gives that country the larger Hala'ib Triangle. Under both positions, nobody claims Bir Tawil. On 16 June 2014, his daughter's seventh birthday, Virginia farmer Jeremiah Heaton planted a blue flag there and declared the Kingdom of North Sudan so that she could be a princess. He said he sought permission from Cairo to make the trip. He later applied for UN observer status and offered honorary titles for $25 and naming rights to a capital city for $1.75m. Durham University geographer Noam Leshem told Al Jazeera that the land's status is ambiguous and that tribes still use it. No government recognised the kingdom.
mechanism: Tests whether a private person can acquire land nobody's government claims; a flag and a website produced no recognition, and terra nullius (land belonging to no state) remained open only to states.

sources.t: Creating the Kingdom of North Sudan (Al Jazeera)
American Man Plants Flag in Remote Sudanese Region (Slate)

name: Later Bir Tawil claimants
founder: Suyash Dixit; Dmitry Zhikharev; Nadera Nassif; Dwain Coward
pop: No residents; artisanal gold miners work the area seasonally
story: Heaton was the first of a run of people to claim Bir Tawil. In November 2017 Suyash Dixit, a 24-year-old businessman from Indore in India, flew from Cairo to Abu Simbel, drove in on 4 November, planted sunflower seeds and declared the Kingdom of Dixit, asking the United Nations for recognition. A day later the Russian Dmitry Zhikharev announced a Kingdom of Middle Earth and accused Heaton and Dixit of faking their visits, saying he had declared himself ruler there in December 2014. In September 2019 a group whose prime minister was named as the Michigan businesswoman Nadera Nassif announced a Kingdom of the Yellow Mountain. Most claims were made online from elsewhere. The London barrister Dwain Coward told VICE he had set up a company in Sudan and sent terms to tribal chiefs, because gold miners using mercury were damaging the land. VICE reports that the only people working there are migrants from Sudan who dig for gold and sell it in Khartoum. No government or international body has recognised any of these claims.
mechanism: Rival private claims to the same land have no referee, because only states can settle title and no state is a party.

sources.t: The Battle for the Last Unclaimed Land on Earth (VICE)

name: Free Republic of Liberland
stopped_by: Croatian police, who block access and dismantled the 2023 camp
pop: No residents on the land; supporters camped there in 2023 and later on a river island
currency: Merit, a cryptocurrency; bitcoin and gold also promoted
passports: Sold to paying supporters; Wikipedia gives $10,000, Wired gives $5,000 or equivalent for full citizenship
laws: Blockchain-based registry and voting planned
challenge: Failed on the ground: Croatia arrested the founder and banned him for five years
cost: Citizenship fee of $5,000 or more; about 1,000 people had paid by 2023
story: After Yugoslavia broke up, Serbia placed its border on the deepest channel of the Danube, while Croatia used old land records that follow the river's 19th-century course. That left pockets on the west bank that neither side claims. On 13 April 2015 the Czech politician Vit Jedlicka planted a flag on the largest, 7 square kilometres of floodplain called Gornja Siga, and declared a state with optional tax. Croatia treats the land as part of an unsettled border dispute, says visitors must obey Croatian law, and has detained them since May 2015. Jedlicka spent a night in custody and was fined. In August 2023, after Croatia entered the Schengen free-travel area, supporters built wooden shelters. Police arrested Jedlicka on 9 September and banned him from Croatia for five years. On 21 September a private company under police watch dismantled and removed the camp; settlers moved to houseboats and a village on the Serbian side. Wired reported that 700,000 people had registered support, about 6,000 were paying e-residents, and nobody lived there.
mechanism: A gap between two states' border claims does not make land free to take, because the state in physical control can treat entry as illegal border crossing whatever the title position.

sources.t: A Crypto Micronation's Future Hangs on a Border Dispute (Wired)
Croatian Police Cross Schengen Border, Liberland Settlement Dismantled (Total Croatia News)
Would-Be Microstate Liberland Keeps Up Its Fight (RFE/RL)

name: Kingdom of Enclava
stopped_by: Slovenian foreign ministry statement, then the 2017 arbitration award on the parcel
challenge: Slovenia and Croatia both said the land was theirs; a 2017 arbitration ruling assigned the parcel to Slovenia
story: The border between Slovenia and Croatia near the village of Brezovica pri Metliki is unusually tangled, with a small Croatian enclave, meaning a piece of one country surrounded by another, already sitting inside Slovenian land. In 2015 the Polish tourist Piotr Wawrzynkiewicz read on Wikipedia that a small piece of land there was unclaimed, and he declared it the Kingdom of Enclava. Newspapers around the world reported the story. The Slovenian foreign ministry then said the plot was part of a territorial claim of its own, also claimed by Croatia, which was going before the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague. That court ruled on 29 June 2017 that a disputed 2.4-hectare parcel beside the enclave belonged to Slovenia, which created a second Croatian enclave. Wawrzynkiewicz moved his project to an unclaimed area on the Croatia-Serbia border. The case shows how a map gap may be only an unfinished dispute. An online reference page called the land unclaimed while two governments were arguing over it in an international forum.
mechanism: An apparent gap on a map can turn out to be land under active dispute, so that the claimant's terra nullius argument collapses as soon as the states speak.

name: Free Republic of Verdis
stopped_by: Croatian police, October 2023
pop: None; a settlement lasted a few days in October 2023
passports: About 350 to 400 issued to accepted applicants; Jackson says some have been used at borders
laws: Citizenship criteria set by founders
challenge: Failed on the ground: settlers arrested, founder banned for life from Croatia
story: Verdis is a 128-acre strip of forest and marsh on the Danube between Croatia and Serbia, known as Pocket 3, roughly the size of Vatican City. Daniel Jackson, born in Australia to British parents, had the idea at about 14 and helped declare the state in 2019, after finding the plot through people he met online. He said it was intended as a neutral hub for humanitarian groups, and that Liberland partly inspired it. He told NBC the group planted a flag in 2023 and carried out surveying. In October 2023 settlers tried to set up a permanent camp. Jackson said Croatian authorities destroyed it within days, arrested the group and told them to leave or be deported. He received a permanent ban from Croatia and the others received three-month bans. He now runs the project from Dover in England and says he plans a legal fight. Verdis had received about 15,000 citizenship applications at $16 each and accepted about 350 to 400. No government recognises it.
mechanism: Repeats the Liberland result at smaller scale: Croatia's physical control of the bank decides who may stay, regardless of who holds formal title.

sources.t: Viva Verdis: Man declares country in unclaimed pocket of land (NBC News)
British teen president of Balkan microstate removed by Croatian police (LBC)

name: Neutral Moresnet
stopped_by: Germany annexed it in 1915; the Treaty of Versailles gave it to Belgium
passports: Residents treated as stateless; none issued
laws: Napoleonic civil and penal codes; visiting Belgian and Prussian judges
challenge: Lasted 104 years until the First World War ended neutrality
recognition: Created and run jointly by neighbouring states
story: After Napoleon's defeat, the Netherlands and Prussia could not agree who should get a valuable zinc mine, called Vieille Montagne or Altenberg. On 26 June 1816 they split the Moresnet district in three and left the mine and its village as a neutral triangle of 3.5 square kilometres, run by one commissioner from each side. Belgium took over the Dutch role after 1830. Old Napoleonic law stayed in force and foreign judges came in to hear cases because the territory had no court. The mine company dominated life, running housing, shops, a hospital and a bank. Taxes were low, there were no import tariffs, and residents counted as stateless. Population rose from 256 in 1815 to 4,668 in 1914. In 1903 a casino opened and closed after pressure from Kaiser Wilhelm II. In 1908 the mine doctor Wilhelm Molly proposed an Esperanto-speaking state named Amikejo, and a rally was held on 13 August. Prussia annexed the territory in 1915, and Versailles gave it to Belgium from January 1920.
mechanism: A gap can last for generations if the neighbouring states agree to leave it open, but it ends when one of them changes its mind.

name: Republic of Indian Stream
founder: Assembly of settlers; Luther Parker among constitution drafters
stopped_by: Coos County sheriff and New Hampshire militia
laws: Written constitution, elected assembly, Justice of the Peace
challenge: Failed: gave way under threat of military occupation
story: The top of the New Hampshire border was unclear, because it depended on which stream counted as the northwesternmost head of the Connecticut River. Britain and the United States each claimed the land, and both sent tax collectors and debt-collecting sheriffs. To stop paying twice, about 300 settlers formed an assembly, declared independence on 9 July 1832 and wrote a constitution. Luther Parker, one of the drafters, served as Justice of the Peace. They meant this to last until the two powers settled the border. The Coos County sheriff kept acting there. On 30 July 1835 he asked for the militia, and two infantry companies gathered at nearby Stewartstown. On 4 August he met 30 to 40 assembly members and gave them an ultimatum. Most gave in. The next day five leaders told a British official that help had not arrived in time and that they had accepted annexation by New Hampshire. The area later became the town of Pittsburg.
mechanism: A self-government formed in a boundary gap holds only until one of the claiming powers is willing to use force, which ended this one without a shot.

name: Republic of Cospaia
founder: Local inhabitants, after a treaty drafting error
stopped_by: Tuscany and the Papal States, by agreed partition in 1826
laws: No taxes or standing government, by local accounts
challenge: Tolerated for nearly four centuries, then partitioned by agreement
recognition: Accepted by Florence and the Papal States from 1484
story: In 1440 Pope Eugene IV, short of money, handed the Sansepolcro district to Florence as security for a debt of 25,000 ducats. The treaty set the new border at a creek called the Rio. Two creeks with that name ran about 500 metres apart, and each side took the one nearer to itself. A strip of 330 hectares around the village of Cospaia ended up belonging to neither. Its roughly 250 inhabitants declared themselves independent, with the motto Perpetua et firma libertas, which is still written over the church door. Florence and the Papal States accepted this in 1484, finding it cheaper than redrawing the border. Goods passed through free of tariffs. After tobacco reached the area in 1574, and after a papal ban on it in 1624, Cospaia gave its farmland to the crop. The two neighbours agreed to divide it in 1826, complaining of smugglers. Fourteen family heads signed their submission in exchange for a silver coin each and permission to grow up to half a million tobacco plants a year.
mechanism: A drafting error can create real independence if both neighbours find it cheaper to tolerate than to fix, and the toleration can be withdrawn by them at any time.

name: Free State of Bottleneck
currency: Local emergency money printed by the territory
laws: Local administration under an elected president
challenge: Ended by events, without a contest
story: After the 1918 Armistice, Allied armies occupied Germany west of the Rhine and marked out three half-circles of 30 kilometres radius on the eastern bank, around Cologne, Koblenz and Mainz. The compass arcs for the French and American zones did not quite meet. That left a narrow gap holding the Wisper valley, the towns of Lorch and Kaub and several villages. With occupied zones on two sides, the Rhine to the south-west, and no road or railway running north-east, the area was cut off from the rest of Germany and its government. Locals declared a free state on 10 January 1919 and named it after the bottleneck shape on the map. About 17,000 people lived there. Lorch was the capital, and its mayor, Edmund Pnischeck, was elected president and headed the administration throughout. The territory issued its own emergency money, with a verse saying nowhere was finer than the Free State of Bottleneck. It lasted until 1 July 1920, by the dates given in the source reviewed here, although the page heading gives 1923 as the end.
mechanism: Shows that a geometric error in a military map can leave a population ungoverned, and that people will build a government within days to fill the gap.

name: No Man's Land and Cimarron Territory
founder: Settlers; Owen G. Chase led the 1886-87 Cimarron Territory effort
stopped_by: Oklahoma Territory absorbed it in 1890
laws: Settlers surveyed their own claims and petitioned for territorial status
challenge: Petitions for territorial status in 1887 did not produce a Cimarron Territory; the strip was absorbed
story: When Texas joined the United States, federal law barred slavery north of latitude 36 degrees 30 minutes. Under the Compromise of 1850, Texas gave up its land north of that line. Other laws then fixed New Mexico's boundary at the 103rd meridian and Kansas's at the 37th parallel in 1854. A strip about 170 miles long was left in no state or territory until 1890. It was officially the Public Land Strip and commonly No Man's Land. Cattlemen moved in after the Civil War and made their own rules for land and disputes. In 1885 the US Supreme Court ruled the strip was not part of the Cherokee Outlet. In 1886 Interior Secretary L.Q.C. Lamar declared it public domain and open to squatter's rights. Since it had never been surveyed, the Homestead Act could not apply, but thousands of settlers came anyway and surveyed it themselves. They organised as Cimarron Territory, with Owen G. Chase at its head, and petitioned Congress in February and December 1887. The strip was joined to Oklahoma Territory, ending its no-government status in 1890.
mechanism: Land can sit inside a country's borders while belonging to no local government; people could live there for decades without valid title, and only the national legislature could end the gap.

name: Couto Misto
stopped_by: Spain and Portugal, by the 1864 Treaty of Lisbon
laws: Popular assembly; right to grant asylum and refuse foreign troops
challenge: Lasted until two neighbours partitioned it by treaty
recognition: Tolerated in practice by Spain and Portugal
story: Couto Misto was a group of three villages on the Spanish-Portuguese border: Santiago de Rubiás, Rubiás and Meaus, in what is now Ourense in Galicia, plus a small uninhabited strip. A couto was a medieval district marked by boundary stones and exempt from the king's authority, with its own economic and legal arrangements. Through overlapping feudal ties this one escaped control by both kingdoms for centuries. Its origin is unclear; one source dates it to the 10th century. Portugal abolished its coutos between 1692 and 1790, and this one was then freed from feudal ties and ran as an independent state in practice. It covered about 26.7 square kilometres and had about 1,000 people by an 1859 estimate. Residents did not pay tax or serve in either army, could grant asylum to outsiders, and could refuse entry to foreign troops. Decisions came from a popular assembly. The Treaty of Lisbon, dated 29 September 1864, divided the territory. Spain took the three villages and most of the land, Portugal took the uninhabited strip, and annexation was completed in 1868.
mechanism: Shows that long custom can produce working self-rule, while also showing that custom gives no protection once neighbouring states agree by treaty to end it.

sources.t: Treaty of Lisbon record (UN Treaty Collection)

name: Clipperton Island arbitration
founder: France, by a naval officer's proclamation in 1858
stopped_by: King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy, as arbitrator, awarding the island to France
pop: No stable population; three guano collectors in 1897
challenge: France won the arbitration against Mexico
recognition: Award accepted as binding by both parties
story: Clipperton is an uninhabited Pacific atoll. On 17 November 1858 the French naval lieutenant Victor le Coat de Kerwéguen, on a merchant ship half a mile offshore, proclaimed French sovereignty forever. A boat landed a few men, nobody left any sign of possession, and notice was sent to the Hawaiian government and printed in the Honolulu newspaper The Polynesian on 8 December. Nothing further happened until 1897, when France found three men collecting guano for an American company. A Mexican gunboat arrived that December, replaced the American flag with Mexico's, and Mexico claimed the island as Spanish inheritance. The two countries agreed on 2 March 1909 to ask the King of Italy to decide. His award, dated 28 January 1931, found Mexico had not proved prior title, so the island was territorium nullius, meaning land belonging to no state, in 1858. Physical possession is normally required, he said, but on a completely uninhabited island a state's arrival can complete it at once. France lost nothing through 39 years of inaction, because it never intended to abandon the island.
mechanism: On a completely uninhabited territory, a state's clear intention, publicity and a brief presence can be enough to take title, and later absence does not lose it unless the state means to abandon the land.

sources.t: Clipperton Island award, UN Reports of International Arbitral Awards vol. II

name: Island of Palmas case
founder: Dispute between the United States and the Netherlands
stopped_by: Arbitrator Max Huber, Permanent Court of Arbitration
challenge: The Netherlands won
story: Palmas, now Miangas in Indonesia, is an island about 2.6 kilometres long. In 1898 Spain ceded the Philippines to the United States by a treaty whose boundaries took in Palmas. In 1906 the United States found that the Netherlands also claimed it. On 23 January 1925 the two countries agreed to binding arbitration, and the Swiss lawyer Max Huber sat as sole arbitrator. The United States argued that Spain had discovered the island, that the island lay close to the Philippines, and that it had inherited Spain's rights. Huber decided on 4 April 1928. He wrote that seeing land gives at most an inchoate title, a starting claim that must be completed by actual possession within a reasonable time. He rejected contiguity, the idea that nearness alone gives ownership. He held that the continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title, and the Dutch had shown this from 1700 to 1906. The island forms in its entirety a part of Netherlands territory.
mechanism: Title to territory comes from continuous and peaceful display of state authority; discovery alone and geographic nearness do not prevail against it.

sources.t: Island of Palmas award, UN Reports of International Arbitral Awards vol. II

name: Sapodilla Cayes
founder: Belize, as applicant at the International Court of Justice
laws: Administered by Belize
challenge: Pending at the International Court of Justice
recognition: Administered by Belize; also claimed by Honduras and affected by a Guatemalan claim
story: The Sapodilla Cayes are a small uninhabited atoll in the Gulf of Honduras, administered by Belize as a marine reserve. They are often thought of as a leftover scrap of land, yet three states have an interest in them. Honduras claims them in its 1982 constitution, and Guatemala claims a maritime boundary north-west of them. On 16 November 2022 Belize went to the International Court of Justice against Honduras, saying the cayes have been part of its territory since the early 19th century, first as the settlement of Belize, then the colony of British Honduras, and since 1981 as an independent state. Guatemala applied on 1 December 2023 for permission to join. Public hearings on that request ran from 24 to 26 November 2025. The court's case page lists a judgment for 19 March 2026 granting Guatemala permission to intervene as a non-party. A decision on who owns the cayes was not listed on the page retrieved for this record.
mechanism: Tiny uninhabited land is rarely terra nullius in practice; any claim can be pulled into state-to-state litigation at the world court.

sources.t: Belize institutes proceedings against Honduras (ICJ press release)
Sovereignty over the Sapodilla Cayes case page (ICJ)

name: Kowloon Walled City
founder: Created by the 1898 lease that excluded it; grew through refugees and residents
stopped_by: British and Chinese governments, by joint decision in 1987
laws: Near-ungoverned; triads controlled it from the 1950s to the 1970s; unlicensed clinics and schools
challenge: Survived a 1948 eviction attempt; ended by joint British-Chinese decision
recognition: Both Britain and China avoided asserting control
cost: HK$2.7bn (US$350m) in compensation to clear residents
story: The Walled City began as a Chinese fort, rebuilt in 1847 after Britain took Hong Kong Island. When Britain leased the New Territories in 1898, the lease left out the fort, so it stayed a Chinese enclave inside British Hong Kong. In 1933 Hong Kong announced plans to clear it and rehouse 436 squatters. After a failed attempt to drive people out in 1948, the British adopted a hands-off approach in most matters. Neither government wanted to enforce its authority, so refugees from the Chinese Civil War poured in. From the 1950s to the 1970s triads controlled the place, with gambling, prostitution and drug trafficking, until police raids in the 1970s reduced their power. Residents ran small factories, schools, and clinics and dental practices with no regulation. By 1987 about 33,000 people lived on 2.6 hectares, some 1.2 million per square kilometre. The two governments announced demolition on 14 January 1987 after laying the ground in the 1984 Joint Declaration. Compensation cost HK$2.7 billion. Demolition ran from March 1993 to April 1994.
mechanism: When two states each decline to exercise authority over a place, the vacuum is filled by residents and criminal groups, and the state's formal claim remains usable whenever it agrees to act.

name: Kingdom of Araucania and Patagonia
stopped_by: Chilean authorities, who arrested, jailed and deported him
pop: Mapuche people of the region; he had support from several leaders
laws: Hereditary constitutional monarchy by decree
challenge: Failed: court in Santiago declared him insane and he was expelled
recognition: None; he had support from some Mapuche leaders
story: Antoine de Tounens was a former lawyer from Perigueux in France who decided to go to Araucania after reading the epic poem La Araucana. He reached Chile in 1858 and met Mapuche leaders south of the Biobio River, promising guns and French help to keep them independent of Chile. Some leaders, including Kilapan and Kalfukura, backed him, possibly believing a European could help their cause. On 17 and 20 November 1860 he issued two decrees saying Araucania and eastern Patagonia did not depend on any other state, and naming himself King Orelie-Antoine I. He named Perquenco his capital, created a flag and had coins minted. Chile's president authorised his arrest, which came on 5 January 1862. A Santiago court declared him insane on 2 September 1862, and he was expelled to France on 28 October. He tried three more times to return and was captured and sent back each time. The source says his declaration led to the Chilean occupation of Araucania, and that he died of ill health caused by his captivity.
mechanism: A claim that land is free ignored both its Indigenous inhabitants' rights and Chile's ability to enforce its own sovereignty by arrest and a court order.

name: Kingdom of Sedang
stopped_by: French Navy, which blocked his return and seized his arms
pop: Bahnar, Rengao and Sedang peoples of the region
laws: Noble titles and orders handed out; postage stamps created
challenge: Failed: France blocked him at sea
recognition: None; France, Britain and Belgium declined or stayed silent
story: Charles-Marie David de Mayrena was a former French official, allegedly involved in embezzlement, who owned a plantation in French Indochina in 1888. When Siam began claiming land near French holdings, he convinced a worried colonial official to send him inland to negotiate with local peoples. On arrival he instead persuaded the chiefs to form a kingdom under him. He argued that the tribes were not subjects of the emperor of Annam, the ruling state in what is now central Vietnam, and so were entitled to independence. The chiefs of the Bahnar, Rengao and Sedang elected him, and on 3 June 1888 he took the title Marie the First. His capital was the village of Kon Gung. He offered to hand his kingdom to France for a trade monopoly and hinted that Prussia was interested. France did not respond, and Britain turned him away in Hong Kong. In Belgium in 1889 a financier offered weapons and money for mineral rights. The French Navy blockaded Vietnamese ports and seized the arms in Singapore.
mechanism: Calling a people independent of the nearest empire does not produce a state when a colonial power controls the sea routes and refuses recognition.

name: Republic of Madawaska
stopped_by: Baker was arrested in 1827; the border settlement came in 1842
challenge: Failed: leader arrested within three months
story: The Treaty of Paris left the border between the United States and British North America unclear in what is now northern Maine and New Brunswick. The Madawaska settlement on the Saint John River sat in the overlap and had 2,487 people in the 1830 census. An American settler, John Baker, arrived in 1817 and lived near what is now Baker Brook. In 1825 he petitioned Maine to take the settlement in. Convinced the land was American, he began provoking the British. In 1827 he tried to stop mail being carried by canoe to Quebec and tried to persuade French residents to reject British authority. A republic was declared on 4 July 1827, with Baker given the title General. He was arrested on 25 September 1827. The wider overlap remained disputed until 1842. Today the communities it covered sit in New Brunswick, Maine and Quebec. The source calls it a putative republic, meaning one that was claimed without ever being shown to work as a government.
mechanism: A declaration made in a boundary overlap can be used as a pressure tactic by one neighbour's supporters, and arrest by the other neighbour ends it.

name: Republic of Lakotah
founder: Russell Means and the Lakota Freedom Movement
laws: Provisional government named by the delegation
challenge: Never tested in court; US law and tribal governments continued unchanged
recognition: None; recognised Lakota tribal governments did not support it
story: On 17 December 2007 four activists calling themselves the Lakota Freedom Delegation went to Washington, D.C., and contacted the State Department. Their leader was Russell Means, a long-time member of the American Indian Movement, who called himself chief facilitator of a provisional government. They said the Lakota were withdrawing unilaterally from treaties their ancestors had signed with the United States. The proposed republic used the borders of the 1851 Treaty of Fort Laramie, covering thousands of square miles in North and South Dakota, Nebraska, Wyoming and Montana. Those lands now hold reservations and non-Native towns. The group cited what it called the colonial apartheid of the reservation system, along with unemployment, poverty and disease, and persistent US treaty violations. None of the existing, recognised Lakota tribal governments supported the proposal, and they were not consulted. The case differs from the unclaimed-land cases because the claim rests on treaty rights of a people already living on the land.
mechanism: A treaty-based claim by a named people has a stronger historic footing than a flag on empty land, but withdrawal needs backing from that people's own governing bodies and a state willing to respond.

name: Grand Duchy of Westarctica
pop: Nobody on the land; over 5,000 online members in 2018
passports: Fantasy passports from 2004, stopped after a Kenyan scammer sold them to refugees as real
laws: Titles of nobility; US non-profit since 2014
challenge: Never tested in Antarctica; Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty bars new claims
story: Marie Byrd Land is about 1.6 million square kilometres of West Antarctica, the one large area no country claims. In 2001 Travis McHenry, a US Navy intelligence specialist, read in the CIA World Factbook that no state had claimed it, and he declared the Protectorate of Westarctica. He wrote letters to many countries; only other micronations responded with recognition. In 2004 he started issuing fantasy passports as souvenirs and stopped after learning that a scammer in Kenya was selling them to refugees as legal travel documents. By 2006 his Navy superiors knew he was writing to foreign governments and told him to choose. He kept his job and gave the title of Grand Duke to a friend, Philip Karns. He returned to the title in 2010, and in 2014 registered Westarctica as a non-profit that campaigns on climate. In July 2025 Indian police arrested Harsh Vardhan Jain for running a fake Westarctica embassy from a rented house in Ghaziabad. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty forbids any new claim while the treaty is in force.
mechanism: Even the one large unclaimed area of Antarctica cannot be claimed under the Antarctic Treaty, and a private claim's documents can be abused by others as real papers.

sources.t: The Antarctic Treaty (Secretariat of the Antarctic Treaty)

name: Grand Duchy of Flandrensis
pop: Nobody on the land; 741 online citizens in 2021
laws: Constitution; yearly elections until 2014; Belgian non-profit since 2021
challenge: Never tested
recognition: None, and the founder says recognition is not the aim
story: Flandrensis began on 4 September 2008 as a two-week hobby by Niels Vermeersch, in Belgium, drawing on the medieval County of Flanders. It claims five islands off West Antarctica: Siple, Cherry, Maher, Pranke and Carney. It has identity cards, a currency, a newspaper, a constitution, an anthem and a football team. Until 2014 it ran partly as a political simulation with parties and yearly elections. It has since described itself as an ecological project to draw attention to melting ice, and in 2021 it registered in Belgium as a non-profit named vzw Groothertogdom Flandrensis. That year it counted 741 citizens from 71 nationalities. Its activity outside the internet has been around Roeselare and Sint-Juliaan in Belgium. It says it does not seek diplomatic recognition, does not intend to visit its islands, and is the only country that wants no humans on its land. It has sent representatives to micronation meetings and co-hosted the first European MicroCon at Ypres in August 2023. The founder spoke at the ChangeNOW climate summit in Paris in May 2022.
mechanism: A claim to unoccupiable land can be used as a publicity tool for conservation, with no attempt to acquire legal title at all.

name: Kingdom of Talossa, Antarctic claim
pop: 157 active citizens in 2023, none on the claimed Antarctic land
laws: Own language with a claimed 35,000 root words
challenge: Never tested
story: Talossa was founded on 26 December 1979 by 14-year-old Robert Ben Madison in his bedroom in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, shortly after his mother died. He took the name after finding it means inside the house in Finnish. Through his teens he produced a handwritten newspaper, a flag and an emblem, with about a dozen relatives and friends as members. In 1980 he began inventing a Talossan language, which now claims 35,000 root words. Talossa has had a website since 1995, and that web presence helped inspire later internet micronations. Its claim covers the east side of Milwaukee, the small French island of Cezembre, and a part of Marie Byrd Land in Antarctica. In 2000 Wired described it as one of the projects that claim territory but would not take power if offered it. On 5 August 2023 it counted 157 active citizens and 564 registered people in all. The pin on this map sits on the Antarctic claim; the people live elsewhere. No state or UN body recognises any of the territory claimed.
mechanism: Adding Antarctic land to a hobby state costs nothing and changes nothing, because no one can inspect, contest or use the claim.

sources.t: It's Good to Be King (Wired, March 2000)

name: Greenpeace World Park Base
stopped_by: Greenpeace itself closed it in 1991 and removed it in 1991-92
laws: None of its own; located in the New Zealand-claimed Ross Dependency
challenge: Not challenged by force; treaty states were reported to ignore it
recognition: Treaty states officially ignored it; New Zealand would have helped in an emergency
story: From 1987 Greenpeace ran a year-round base at Cape Evans on Ross Island, in the part of Antarctica New Zealand claims. It remains the only non-government year-round base there has been. The aim was to give the group standing at Antarctic Treaty meetings and to find allies for stopping mineral extraction and making the continent a World Park. At the time, treaty states were negotiating a mining convention called CRAMRA. A British Antarctic Survey account says Greenpeace and other groups challenged the treaty states with unprecedented public scrutiny in the 1980s. Australia and France then withdrew from the mining convention, and it failed to get enough support by 25 November 1989. A new environmental protocol was agreed in 1991 and came into force in 1998. Greenpeace closed the base in 1991 and removed it in 1991-92. A study in Polar Record estimated total fuel spills at under 200 litres, with contamination in one spot reaching 70 centimetres into the permafrost. Treaty governments had officially ignored the base and given no assistance.
mechanism: A non-state group gained political leverage in Antarctica by occupying a site and campaigning from it, without claiming any land.

sources.t: Monitoring and remediation at former World Park Base (Polar Record)
30th anniversary of the Environmental Protocol (British Antarctic Survey)

name: Seven Antarctic claims and Article IV
founder: Argentina, Australia, Chile, France, New Zealand, Norway, United Kingdom
pop: Rotating research staff; small family settlements
laws: Antarctic Treaty, signed 1959, in force 1961; 58 parties
challenge: Claims frozen, neither ended nor accepted
recognition: Other states do not recognise the claims; the US and Russia keep a basis of claim
story: Seven countries have made eight claims to parts of Antarctica. Britain went first in 1908, saying it needed to regulate and tax whaling. New Zealand's claim dates to 1923, Australia's to 1933, Norway's to Peter I Island to 1931 and Queen Maud Land to 1939, Chile's to 1940, and Argentina's to the 1940s. The claims of Argentina, Chile and Britain overlap. In 1943 Britain began Operation Tabarin to put people on the ground and support its position. Twelve countries signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington on 1 December 1959, and it came into force in 1961. It now has 58 parties. Article IV freezes the question: no act while the treaty is in force can support or deny a claim, or create sovereignty rights, and no new claim or enlargement can be made. Other countries do not recognise the claims, while the United States and Russia keep a basis of claim. Countries without claims, such as China and India, run stations on land others claim. Marie Byrd Land stays unclaimed.
mechanism: Article IV shows that a territorial question can be frozen by treaty, with all sides keeping their positions and nothing done during the freeze counting for or against them.

sources.t: The Antarctic Treaty (Secretariat of the Antarctic Treaty)

name: Villa Las Estrellas
pop: 150 in summer and 80 in winter; 41 in a 2013 count of the civilian settlement
laws: Chilean law; civil registry, school, bank
challenge: Not challenged directly; lies in land also claimed by Argentina and Britain
recognition: Chile's Antarctic claim not generally recognised
story: Villa Las Estrellas is a Chilean civilian settlement on King George Island, attached to the Eduardo Frei air base. People moved in on 15 February 1984, and it was formally founded on 9 April that year, with a school opening the same day. It later gained a civil registry, post office, bank, library and church. Fourteen family homes stand there. Chile treats it as part of the commune of Antartica in its southern Magallanes region. Argentina and Britain also claim the land. Juan Pablo Camacho, born there in November 1984, was the first Chilean born in Antarctic territory. In a ceremony at the presidential palace on 24 November, Augusto Pinochet gave him life insurance and funding for his studies. The local radio station is named Radio Soberania, meaning sovereignty. BBC Future reported in 2018 that residents on long stays have their appendix removed before coming, since the nearest major hospital is over 1,000 kilometres away. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says nothing done there can strengthen a claim.
mechanism: Families, a school and a civil registry are the normal evidence of state presence, but Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says they cannot add to Chile's legal claim while the treaty lasts.

sources.t: The Antarctic town where families must have surgery (BBC Future)

name: Esperanza Base births
pop: 56 in winter, including 10 families and 2 teachers
passports: Children take their parents' nationality; there is no Antarctic passport
laws: Argentine civil register office and provincial school
challenge: Not challenged directly; the land is also claimed by Chile and Britain
recognition: Argentina's claim is not generally recognised
story: Argentina built Esperanza Base near the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula in 1953, on land also claimed by Chile and Britain. It was the scene of the 1952 Hope Bay incident, when an Argentine party fired a machine gun over the heads of a British team, reportedly the only shots fired in anger on the continent. In late 1977 Silvia Morella de Palma, seven months pregnant and the wife of the army detachment's commander, was flown to the base. Her son Emilio Marcos Palma was born on 7 January 1978, weighing 3.4 kilograms, and was baptised in the base chapel. ExplorersWeb describes the flight as part of an Argentine initiative to strengthen its territorial presence. Because Britain also claimed the land, he was also entitled to British citizenship. Marisa Delgado followed on 27 May 1978. Some sources count 11 Antarctic births in all, mostly at Esperanza and Chile's Frei base. Today the base has a school, founded in 1978, and a civil register that records births and marriages. Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty stops such acts from building a legal claim.
mechanism: Births and civil registers are classic evidence of a state's authority over land, but Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty says acts done during the treaty cannot support a claim.

sources.t: Born in Antarctica: The White Continent Has 11 Citizens (ExplorersWeb)
The Antarctic Treaty (Secretariat of the Antarctic Treaty)

name: Svalbard Treaty
laws: Norwegian sovereignty with treaty limits; separate budget; limited taxes
challenge: Stable since 1925; Russia keeps settlements under its treaty rights
story: Svalbard, an Arctic archipelago twice the size of Belgium, was a terra nullius, meaning land belonging to no state, until the 20th century. Whalers, then miners, from many countries worked there with almost no law, and disputes between miners and owners created demand for a government. The Treaty signed in Paris on 9 February 1920 recognised Norway's full and unqualified sovereignty. It came into force on 14 August 1925, after Japan became the last original signatory to ratify. In exchange Norway accepted limits. Citizens and companies of every treaty party may live there and have equal rights to fish, hunt and do business, including mining. Norway may tax only enough to pay for running Svalbard, so its budget stays apart from the mainland's. Article 9 bans naval bases and fortifications, and the islands are visa-free. Russia uses its rights through its settlements at Barentsburg and Pyramiden. There were 14 original parties and 49 by 2026. About 2,500 people live there, and Norway has run the administration since the treaty took effect.
mechanism: Land without a sovereign can be handed to one state by treaty while other states keep guaranteed rights of access, a working model of shared economic use under a single government.

sources.t: Genesis of the Spitsbergen/Svalbard Treaty (Cambridge History of the Polar Regions)

name: Russia's 2007 North Pole flag
founder: Russian expedition led by Artur Chilingarov
laws: High seas beyond national zones; UN Convention on the Law of the Sea sets the seabed process
challenge: Rejected as a legal act by Canada and the United States
story: On 2 August 2007 a Russian expedition sent two Mir submersibles to the seabed at the North Pole. A mechanical arm placed a rust-proof titanium flag at a depth of 4,261 metres. The research ship Akademik Fedorov carried about 100 scientists, and the leader, parliament member Artur Chilingarov, said people could find the flag in a thousand years. Canada's foreign minister Peter MacKay said this was not the 15th century, when countries could plant flags and claim territory, and a US State Department spokesman said the flag had no legal standing. Lindsay Parson of Britain's National Oceanography Centre told RFE/RL that the 200-nautical-mile zones of the five Arctic coastal states leave a central area of about 300,000 to 400,000 square kilometres unclaimed. Any state wanting the seabed there has to build a scientific case under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, a process separate from flag-planting. He called the dive a scientific achievement that meant very little as a legal claim. Russia's research supported its 2001 territorial submission.
mechanism: Symbolic possession carries no title to the deep seabed; extended claims follow scientific evidence under the Law of the Sea convention.

sources.t: Russia plants flag on Arctic seabed (CNN/Reuters)

name: Arctic Sanctuary and the Greenpeace flag
laws: Proposed; no treaty adopted
challenge: No state adopted it
recognition: European Parliament called for one; not adopted as law
story: The waters at the North Pole lie beyond the national zones of the Arctic coastal states. In April 2013 a team of four young people working with Greenpeace, led by two young Indigenous Arctic people, trekked to the Pole. They cut a hole in the ice on the weekend of 13 April and lowered a flag designed by a child from Malaysia to the seabed about four kilometres down, at the spot where Russia placed its flag in 2007. The flag was attached to a glass and titanium capsule holding the signatures of nearly three million people who asked for the region to be declared a global sanctuary. Greenpeace wanted it protected from oil drilling and mining. In 2008 the European Parliament suggested that a treaty modelled on the Antarctic Treaty might cover the unpopulated and unclaimed area at the centre of the Arctic Ocean. In a 2014 resolution it called for a sanctuary in the waters outside coastal states' zones. No such sanctuary exists on the record reviewed here, and the proposal remains a campaign aim.
mechanism: A global commons with no sovereign has no one able to create a sanctuary alone, so protection depends on states agreeing to a new treaty.

sources.t: Greenpeace plants flag under the Pole (Nunatsiaq News)
Activists plant flag on Arctic seabed (Al Jazeera)

name: Fletcher's Ice Island T-3 and US v. Escamilla
founder: US Air Force, under Col. Joseph O. Fletcher
stopped_by: Station abandoned; the ice drifted on
pop: 19 people in the 1970 team; usually 25 to 30 staff
laws: US federal law asserted; station manager only
challenge: The US court kept jurisdiction, by an evenly split appeal
recognition: Canada took no action and did not state a position on the case
story: T-3 was a drifting iceberg about 11 by 5 kilometres, used as a staffed US research station from 1952 to 1978, with huts, a power plant and an airstrip. On 16 July 1970 Mario Escamilla, armed with a borrowed rifle during a dispute over raisin wine, shot and killed station manager Bennie Lightsey. The island was then at about 84 degrees 47 minutes north, inside the Arctic sector Canada had claimed. Canada chose not to act. US officials flew Escamilla to Dulles Airport in Virginia and charged him on the theory that the ice was on the high seas within US special maritime jurisdiction. A jury convicted him of involuntary manslaughter, and he received three years. In 1972 the Fourth Circuit appeals court split evenly on whether US jurisdiction covered an unclaimed ice island, so the trial court's ruling stayed in place, but it overturned the conviction for other trial errors and ordered a retrial. He was acquitted on retrial. Congress did not settle the jurisdiction issue until a 1984 change to federal law.
mechanism: An unclaimed moving ice island is not clearly land or a ship; the even split left the jurisdiction question open until Congress legislated, and a state's law can follow its nationals only where a court accepts it.

sources.t: United States v. Escamilla, 467 F.2d 341 (4th Cir. 1972)
State Jurisdiction over Ice Island T-3: The Escamilla Case (Arctic journal)

name: Hans Island
stopped_by: Canada, Denmark and Greenland, by agreement on 14 June 2022
laws: Divided by treaty between Canada and Denmark/Greenland
challenge: Settled peacefully
story: Hans Island, called Tartupaluk in Greenlandic, is a bare rock of 1.2 square kilometres in Nares Strait, between Canada's Ellesmere Island and Greenland. In 1973 Canada and Denmark agreed a sea boundary through the strait but could not agree who owned the island. Denmark pointed to an expedition with Danish participation that named the island in 1853, and to its geology and slightly closer position to Greenland. Canada said Denmark's claim had lapsed. In 2005 NPR reported a summer of flag-planting and gift-leaving, and said Denmark sent a warship after Canada's defence minister raised a flag there. On 14 June 2022 the foreign ministers Melanie Joly and Jeppe Kofod and Greenland's premier Mute Egede exchanged bottles of Canadian whisky and Danish bitter. The agreement split the island along a natural ridge, roughly 60 percent to Denmark and the remainder to Canada, which gave the two countries their first land border. It also settled the remaining sea boundary in the Lincoln and Labrador seas.
mechanism: Two states with a live territorial dispute over an uninhabited rock can divide it in half by agreement instead of litigating title, leaving no gap.

sources.t: The Hans Island "Peace" Agreement (Library of Congress, In Custodia Legis)

name: Eastern Greenland case and Erik the Red's Land
stopped_by: Permanent Court of International Justice, 5 April 1933
pop: Uninhabited except for three main Norwegian stations
challenge: Norway lost 12 votes to 2
recognition: None; the Court ruled the occupation invalid
story: By 1931 the east coast of Greenland was uninhabited apart from three main Norwegian stations: Jonsbu, Myggbukta and Antarctic Havn. In June of that year Hallvard Devold, a founder of the Norwegian Arctic Trading Company, raised the Norwegian flag at Myggbukta. On 10 July 1931 Norway issued a royal proclamation occupying the area and named it Erik the Red's Land. Norway's position was that this part of Greenland was terra nullius, land belonging to no state, because Denmark had never effectively occupied it. Denmark went to the Permanent Court of International Justice on 12 July, asking the court to declare the occupation a violation of the legal position and therefore unlawful and invalid. The case also turned on the Ihlen Declaration, in which Norway's foreign minister told the Danish minister in July 1919 that Norway would not make any difficulties over Denmark's claim to all of Greenland. On 5 April 1933, by twelve votes to two, the court found the Norwegian proclamation unlawful and invalid. Norway then abandoned the claim.
mechanism: Thin use of remote land can still be enough for sovereignty when a state has shown authority there; a later proclamation and private stations did not displace Denmark.

sources.t: Legal Status of Eastern Greenland, PCIJ Series A/B No. 53 (1933)

name: Wrangel Island expeditions
stopped_by: Soviet Union, which removed the last colony in 1924
challenge: Failed: Soviet ship removed the settlers
story: Wrangel Island lies in the Arctic Ocean north of Siberia. In 1914 survivors of the crushed ship Karluk, part of an expedition organised by Vilhjalmur Stefansson, were stranded there for nine months. In 1921 Stefansson sent five settlers there, Allan Crawford of Canada, Americans Fred Maurer, Lorne Knight and Milton Galle, and Ada Blackjack, an Inupiat seamstress and cook, in a speculative attempt to claim the island for Canada. He said he wanted to head off a Japanese claim. A relief ship failed to reach them in 1922. In 1923 another ship found only one survivor, Ada Blackjack, and left a new party of 13, the American Charles Wells and 12 Inuit. In 1924 the Soviet Union sent the ship Krasny Oktyabr, or Red October, and removed the settlement, by then 14 people because one child had been born. Wells died of pneumonia in Vladivostok during a diplomatic row over an American boundary marker, and an Inuk child died of tuberculosis. The island stays under Russian control and became a World Heritage Site in 2004.
mechanism: A small private colony on remote land can be removed by the nearest state with a ship, showing that occupation without state support gives no protection.

name: Principality of Hutt River
stopped_by: Founder's son Graeme dissolved it, citing the pandemic
laws: Royal titles for family; no court of its own found
challenge: Lost repeatedly: 1977 tax prosecution, a High Court application dismissed, and a 2017 tax judgment
cost: Courts ordered Casley to pay A$2.7m and his son A$242,000 in unpaid tax in 2017
story: The wheat farmer Leonard Casley had about 4,000 hectares of crop ready when new quotas let him sell only about 40 hectares' worth. On 21 April 1970 he declared his 75-square-kilometre farm, 517 kilometres north of Perth, the independent Hutt River Province. He later said an unanswered letter gave it de facto autonomy in 1972 and began calling himself Prince Leonard. He issued a currency, stamps and passports. On 15 February 1977 he was convicted for failing to give tax documents to the Australian Taxation Office, and that December he declared war on Australia, ending it days later. The High Court of Australia dismissed one of his applications as fatuous, frivolous and vexatious. In June 2017 Justice Rene Le Miere of the Supreme Court of Western Australia rejected the argument that the court had no power over Hutt River and ordered Leonard to pay A$2.7 million and his son Arthur A$242,000. Leonard died in 2019. On 3 August 2020 his son Prince Graeme dissolved it, citing hard times in the pandemic, and the farm went on sale.
mechanism: Australian courts held that a declared secession does not remove a person from national tax law.

sources.t: Hutt River tax row: Prince Leonard and son ordered to pay $3 million (ABC)
Hutt River micronation to rejoin Australia (Guardian via Yahoo)

name: Principality of Seborga
pop: 283 in 2025, within an ordinary Italian town
laws: Prince elected by the town; ministers and motto
challenge: Not tested in the sources reviewed; the town remains an Italian comune
recognition: None confirmed; supporters claim recognition by Burkina Faso
story: Seborga is a Ligurian village near the French border, about 35 kilometres from Monaco. In 1963 Giorgio Carbone, a former flower grower and head of the local growers' cooperative, said documents in the Vatican archives showed Seborga had never belonged to the House of Savoy, so it was wrongly included in the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. Supporters add that the Congress of Vienna overlooked it. The sources describe these as unproven claims. Villagers elected him head of state that year, and he took the title His Tremendousness, Giorgio I. He formed a cabinet, minted a currency called the luigino, and set up a blue and white flag and the Latin motto Sub Umbra Sede, meaning sit in the shade. Sentry boxes stand on the road in. He held the role until his death on 25 November 2009. Marcello Menegatto was elected in 2010, and Nina Menegatto in 2019, with a further seven-year term confirmed on 23 October 2026. Italy continues to treat the village as a comune in Imperia province, and tourism has grown.
mechanism: A historical argument about a lost state, even with popular local support, produces no legal change as long as the national government keeps running the place as an ordinary municipality.

name: Sovereign State of Forvik
stopped_by: Lerwick Sheriff Court rejected his argument in 2011
laws: Declared a Crown dependency
challenge: Lost: sheriff rejected his 71-page challenge to Scottish jurisdiction
story: Stuart Hill, from Essex, was shipwrecked on the one-hectare islet of Forewick Holm in Shetland in 2001 during a failed trip around Britain, and was nicknamed Captain Calamity. He settled in Shetland and argued that the islands were never formally handed to Scotland or Britain. On 21 June 2008 he declared the islet the Sovereign State of Forvik, a British Crown dependency outside the UK and the EU, and in 2010 he helped launch a Sovereign Nation of Shetland. In 2011, aged 68, he was charged with 12 motoring offences, including having no insurance, tax, licence or MOT, on vans he said were consular vehicles for Forvik. At Lerwick Sheriff Court in August he was locked up for 20 minutes after refusing to answer the charges. He then presented a 71-page submission arguing the court had no power in Shetland. Sheriff Graeme Napier spent two days hearing it, called the affair a pantomime, called Hill deluded and seriously misguided, and dismissed the claim, sending him to trial. VICE later found him, aged 73, still campaigning for Shetland to leave the UK.
mechanism: A Scottish sheriff held that historical arguments about how Shetland passed to Scotland do not remove a person from the jurisdiction of the courts or the rules of the road.

sources.t: Hill faces trial after claim dismissed (Shetland News)
Hill handcuffed, then given a hearing (Shetland News)
Captain Calamity and the quest for Shetland independence (VICE)

name: Freetown Christiania
laws: Residents' plenum and working groups; a foundation holds the land
challenge: Survived a 1978 Supreme Court clearance order; later bought the land
recognition: Danish state negotiated with it; no state recognises independence
cost: Residents set up a fund in 2011 to purchase the land; first payment July 2012
story: In 1971 squatters moved into an abandoned military barracks in the Christianshavn district of Copenhagen and set up a community built on free cannabis, limited government, no cars and no police. An article in a local paper proclaimed a free town. The Defence Ministry sued on 1 April 1976, and the Supreme Court ruled on 2 February 1978 that the site should be cleared at once, but this was not carried out. Successive governments tried to close it, often over the open sale of hashish. After hard talks, which at one stage closed the site to the public, residents agreed in June 2011 to set up a fund to buy the land, and with the first payment in July 2012 they became legal owners. About 850 to 1,000 people live there. It draws half a million visitors a year. After repeated shootings, residents and authorities dug up the main dealing lane, Pusher Street, on 6 April 2024, unlocking state money for renovation and for making the area part of the wider city.
mechanism: Fifty years of tolerance, followed by purchase of the land, gave a squat secure legal title inside the state, while it remained fully under Danish law.

sources.t: Denmark shuts down cannabis Pusher Street (CNN)
Christiania wants to rebuild without its hashish market (AP via KTVZ)

name: Free Independent Republic of Frestonia
founder: Squatters of Freston Road; Nicholas Albery proposed independence
stopped_by: Ended as residents formed a housing co-op and negotiated with the council
laws: Referendum, ministers, Latin motto; applied to the UN
challenge: Succeeded in blocking demolition; absorbed through a housing deal
story: Freston Road in west London held rows of condemned Victorian cottages, broken into by squatters from 1974. When the Greater London Council planned to clear the 1.8-acre site, the 120 residents all took the surname Bramley so the council would have to rehouse them together. At a public meeting of 200 people, resident Nicholas Albery suggested seceding, inspired by the film Passport to Pimlico and a visit to Christiania. A referendum showed 94 percent in favour. They declared independence on 31 October 1977, applied to the United Nations and warned that peacekeeping troops might be needed. The actor David Rappaport became foreign minister, playwright Heathcote Williams ambassador to Britain, and a two-year-old child education minister. They issued stamps and visas. Shadow Chancellor Geoffrey Howe sent a supportive letter, and Williams won a court ruling that for a dispute over his play the area was not part of the UK. By 1982 the council had dropped demolition. There were then 23 houses and 97 residents, who formed Bramley's Housing Co-op and negotiated with the council.
mechanism: A secession stunt worked as a negotiating tactic: publicity forced a housing authority to bargain, and the group gained its aim through a co-operative recognised under ordinary law.

sources.t: Republic of Frestonia: How squatters declared independence (The Independent)

name: Republic of Uzupis
founder: Local artists in Vilnius; Romas Lileikis, president
laws: 41-clause constitution, president, government
challenge: No challenge reported; accepted as a local tradition
story: Uzupis is a neighbourhood of Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania, about 60 hectares in size, on the far side of the Vilnele river. Its name means beyond the river. In 1995 local artists used an empty Soviet-era plinth for a statue of Frank Zappa. On 1 April 1997 they declared the district an independent republic. It has a president, Romas Lileikis, a government, and a navy of three or four small boats used for ceremonies. An army of about 10 men has been retired. The constitution was written by Lileikis and a colleague named Cepaitis in about three hours one afternoon in 1998, and has 41 clauses, including a right to hot water because Lileikis had none that day. It has been translated into many languages. On Uzupis Day, 1 April, visitors can have their passports stamped. BBC Travel reports that foreign governments do not recognise it as a nation, while it has become a source of pride in Vilnius. The page reviewed reports no dispute with the Lithuanian state.
mechanism: A state can absorb a self-declared republic at no cost by treating it as culture, since the claim asserts identity and leaves law and taxes untouched.

sources.t: Uzupis: A tiny republic of free spirits (BBC Travel)

name: Republic of Kugelmugel
laws: One address, president
challenge: Founder jailed for 10 weeks in 1979; the city then gave the building "asylum"
story: In 1971 the artist Edwin Lipburger and his son built an eight-metre spherical house near Wiener Neustadt in Lower Austria without a permit. A long dispute with the authorities followed. He declared the sphere an independent republic, with the date given as 19 December 1976, and issued passports. In August 1975 the township of Neudorfl had offered it a home, and moving it by helicopter was discussed, but that did not happen. In 1979 he was sentenced to 10 weeks in prison for unlawful assumption of a public authority, an Austrian offence of acting as an official without the right. In 1982 the building was dismantled and moved to the Prater park in Vienna, where it sits behind tall barbed-wire fences. Mayor Helmut Zilk gave it what was called asylum. The city assumed the object would be temporary, and the legal dispute continued. The republic claims 94 square metres and has a single address, 2 Antifaschismusplatz. Nikolaus Lipburger took over in 2015, and Linda Treiber in 2022 as president.
mechanism: Declaring a building a state does not cure a planning violation, and Austria used a criminal offence against false official acts when the founder pushed it too far.

name: Kingdom of Elleore
pop: Dozens for one week each year; otherwise empty
laws: Mock monarchy with nobility and a yearly enthronement
challenge: Never challenged; private ownership and a parody
story: Elleore is an island of about 15,000 square metres in Roskilde Fjord in Denmark. In 1944, during the German occupation, a group of Copenhagen schoolteachers bought it for a summer camp. They declared it a kingdom as a gentle parody of Denmark's government and royal traditions, and claim a history going back to Irish monks in the 10th century. Prior to this the island was known mainly for the controversial 1907 film Lovejagten, which was shot there. The kingdom has its own traditions, including a ban on the novel Robinson Crusoe and Elleore Standard Time, which runs 12 minutes behind Danish time. Place names, government bodies and noble titles parody the Danish ones. The island is empty apart from a week-long annual gathering called the Elleuge, attended by dozens of citizens, when the reigning monarch is enthroned. The capital, Maglelille, is a town of tents that exists only during that week. Because the founders own the island, the project needed no conflict with the Danish state and the record shows none.
mechanism: Owning land outright gives a group private control and room for parody, and it adds nothing to sovereignty, which remains with the state.

name: Royal Republic of Ladonia
pop: None resident; 22,858 online citizens from over 50 countries in 2020
laws: Queen for life, elected president; own two-word language
challenge: Sculptures survived court challenges; a third was ordered removed in 1999
story: In 1980 the Swedish artist Lars Vilks began building two sculptures on the Kullaberg nature reserve in north-west Skane: Nimis, 75 tonnes of driftwood, and Arx, made of stone. They were so hard to reach that nobody found them for two years. The local council then ruled that they were buildings, which were forbidden on the reserve, and ordered them removed. Vilks appealed repeatedly and lost. In the meantime Joseph Beuys bought Nimis in 1984, and after his death the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude bought it. On 2 June 1996, in protest against the council, Vilks declared the area around Nimis an independent country called Ladonia. In 1999 he built a third sculpture, Omphalos. A foundation complained to the police, and in August 1999 a district court ordered Omphalos removed but refused to order the removal of Nimis and Arx. The foundation appealed to the Supreme Court and lost. Ladonia has a two-word language, and it takes citizenship applications online. It counted 22,858 citizens in 2020, none of whom live there.
mechanism: Declaring a micronation can publicise a planning fight, but it was ordinary property and appeal law that decided what stayed and what went.

name: Republic of Molossia
laws: President, flag, joke laws
challenge: None; he pays local property tax
story: Molossia is 11.3 acres of land near Dayton, Nevada, owned by Kevin Baugh, who calls himself President. He conceived it as a teenager in 1977 with a friend under other names, including the Grand Republic of Vuldstein, and took the current form after he bought the land in 1998. He credits the film The Mouse That Roared and his army service. Visitors pay a customs fee of pocket change, have their passports stamped, and are given money made of paper circles on poker chips. The currency is the Valora, set at 80 US cents. Laws ban onions, spinach and catfish, and setting off a nuclear device carries a 500 Valora fine. The country says it has been in a conflict with East Germany since 1983, on the grounds of drills Baugh did in the US Army. An Independent report gives 27 citizens. Baugh pays property tax to Storey County and calls it foreign aid. He told a reporter that everyone wants to think they have their own country, though the US is much larger.
mechanism: Owning land and paying local tax on it, even under a joke label, avoids the conflict with the state that ended other claims.

name: Aerican Empire
laws: Describes itself as parliamentary, under an Emperor
challenge: None
story: The Aerican Empire is a self-declared monarchy founded in Canada on 8 May 1987 by Eric Lis, then a child, and a group of friends. Its name is a play on American Empire and the founders say it began as humour. For its first ten years it was almost wholly fictional: it claimed a galaxy of invented planets and fought wars with other micronations that never involved physical contact. It went online in 1997, and in 2000 The New York Times called its site one of the more imaginative micronation sites. It issued novelty passports from 2007, and one was shown at a 2007 art exhibition at the Palais de Tokyo in Paris. It issued its first stamps in 2015. Its flag resembles Canada's with a yellow smiling face in place of the red maple leaf. Its mission statement says the Empire exists to help bring about a society in which the Empire is no longer needed. Lis remains Emperor. In 2025 it hosted MicroCon in Montreal, attended by 120 people from 48 micronations.
mechanism: A micronation with a claim that is openly fictional poses no challenge to any state, which is why it can run indefinitely.

name: Sark
founder: Helier de Carteret, by royal grant
laws: Own parliament (Chief Pleas); laws based on Norman law
challenge: Feudal structure was changed in 2008 after a human rights challenge
recognition: Part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a Crown Dependency
story: Sark is a 5.44-square-kilometre island in the Channel Islands with about 500 people. In 1565 Elizabeth I granted it to Helier de Carteret, of Jersey, as a fief on condition that he clear out pirates and keep at least 40 loyal men there. He rented out 40 parcels called tenements. The island's parliament, Chief Pleas, long consisted of the Seigneur, or feudal lord, the Seneschal, the 40 tenement holders and 12 elected deputies. The billionaire brothers David and Frederick Barclay bought the neighbouring islet of Brecqhou in 1993. In the mid-1990s they went to the European Court of Human Rights against Sark's inheritance law, which required their island to pass to David's eldest son. In 1999 women gained equal inheritance rights. The brothers then argued that the whole system broke the European Convention on Human Rights, and it was replaced under a new constitution in 2008. Candidates backed by their businesses won few seats in 2008 and 2010. Sark remains part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, a self-governing British Crown Dependency.
mechanism: Very old self-rule inside a larger legal order can be forced to change by the human rights law that binds that order, showing that autonomy has limits set from outside.

name: Kingdom of Redonda
founder: M.P. Shiel, who credited his father
stopped_by: Nobody; titles continue among writers
laws: Literary titles passed between claimants
challenge: Never contested by the state; the island is part of Antigua and Barbuda
story: Redonda is an uninhabited rock just over a mile long between Nevis and Montserrat, part of Antigua and Barbuda. It has no fresh water apart from rain, and landing is possible only in calm seas. From 1865 to 1912 it was mined for guano, with many thousands of tons of phosphate shipped to Britain. The writer M.P. Shiel claimed his father had founded a Kingdom of Redonda in 1865 and that he himself became king in 1880. In 1936 he passed the title and rights to his work to the London poet John Gawsworth, who held court as King Juan in a Bayswater pub and is said to have handed the title out several times when short of money. It later passed to Wynne-Tyson, who abdicated in 1997 in favour of the Spanish novelist Javier Marias. Rival claimants still dispute it half-seriously. In September 2023 Antigua and Barbuda created the Redonda Ecosystem Reserve across nearly 30,000 hectares, after removing goats and rats from 2016, and the island's vegetation returned.
mechanism: Literary title-passing has no legal effect; Antigua and Barbuda, the real sovereign, used its power to create a large nature reserve on and around the island.

name: Conch Republic
founder: Mayor Dennis Wardlow and the Key West city council
pop: Key West residents; not an actual state population
laws: Tourist festival, secretary general
challenge: Court injunction failed before secession; no challenge to the joke itself
recognition: None; officials were invited to some events as a courtesy
cost: Applied for $1bn in foreign aid as a joke
story: In April 1982 the US Border Patrol set up a roadblock and checkpoint that caused serious inconvenience for residents and tourists in the Florida Keys. Key West's city council complained to the federal government and got no answer, and an attempt to get a court injunction failed. On 23 April 1982, as a protest, Mayor Dennis Wardlow and the council declared Key West independent. Wardlow became prime minister. The new republic declared war on the United States by breaking a stale Cuban loaf over the head of a man in a naval uniform, surrendered to him after one minute, and applied for one billion dollars in foreign aid. The event has been held every 23 April since then, as a week-long festival, and the name has been stretched to cover all the Keys. Conch representatives were invited to the 1994 Summit of the Americas in Miami and the 1995 Florida Jubilee. The organisation calls itself a sovereign state of mind, and it functions mainly as a tourism promoter.
mechanism: Mock secession can bring publicity to a real grievance after ordinary court action fails, without any legal change in status.

name: Prospera ZEDE
aka: Zones for Employment and Economic Development
stopped_by: Honduras: 2022 repeal law and 2024 Supreme Court ruling; project still running while the dispute continues
laws: Own regulations, single-digit taxes, private arbitration with retired Arizona judges
challenge: Legal basis struck down on 20 September 2024; company went to international arbitration
recognition: Granted by a previous Honduran government; later revoked
cost: Claim at ICSID: originally about US$10.775bn, reduced to about US$1.63bn according to the Honduran attorney general (October 2025)
story: In 2013 Honduras amended its constitution to allow ZEDEs, zones with their own laws, courts and taxes, after similar plans called Special Development Regions were struck down as a breach of sovereignty. Erick Brimen, a Venezuelan-born fund manager, applied in 2017 and built Prospera on Roatan island with US venture capital, run through a Delaware company that holds a veto on its council. It offers single-digit taxes, its own regulations, and a court staffed by retired Arizona judges who hear cases online. Neighbours in Crawfish Rock feared losing their land. President Xiomara Castro signed a repeal of the ZEDE law in April 2022, saying Honduras was recovering its sovereignty. On 20 September 2024 the Supreme Court declared the ZEDE laws unconstitutional with retroactive effect. Prospera's owners had already brought a claim of about US$10.7 billion before the World Bank's arbitration centre, ICSID, under a stability agreement and the CAFTA-DR trade deal. Honduras withdrew from ICSID in August 2024. Honduran officials said in October 2025 that the claim had dropped to US$1.63 billion. ICSID lists the case as pending, with a site visit in October 2026.
mechanism: A state can give away lawmaking to a private zone and later reclaim it through its own courts, but investment treaties can let the company pursue damages abroad.

sources.t: Honduras Prospera Inc. v. Republic of Honduras, ICSID Case No. ARB/23/2
Corte Suprema declara inconstitucionales las ZEDE (VOA)
Prospera ZEDE redujo 85% el monto reclamado (Revista E&N)
Libertarian city dream in Honduras becomes $11 billion nightmare (Bloomberg Law)
Honduran economic zones in limbo (LA Times)

name: Dubai International Financial Centre
laws: English-language common-law courts; own regulator (Dubai Financial Services Authority)
challenge: Created by law, not contested
recognition: Created and backed by UAE and Dubai law
story: The DIFC is a 110-hectare financial zone in Dubai. In September 2004 federal law in the United Arab Emirates allowed each emirate to set up the legal structures needed for financial centres. Dubai Law No. 9 of 2004 created the centre, and Dubai Law No. 12 of 2004 created its courts. The DIFC follows common law, the English-style system built on past court rulings, in English, separate from the legal systems of Dubai and of the UAE federal government. It has its own regulator and offers companies a 50-year guarantee of zero tax on corporate income. The courts began working in 2006. A Small Claims Tribunal was added in 2007, hearing cases up to AED 500,000. At first, the courts could only hear cases tied to the zone. On 31 October 2011, Dubai Law No. 16 let them hear any local or international commercial case if all parties agree. The Court of First Instance can act when a contract names it or when parties choose it after a dispute has started. The zone remains part of Dubai.
mechanism: A state can legally switch off its own commercial law inside a defined zone, with no loss of sovereignty, because the zone's powers come from the state's own statutes.

name: Mount Athos
founder: Orthodox monks; present since at least the 9th century
pop: Monks of 20 monasteries; number not confirmed in sources read
passports: Entry permit from the Pilgrims' Bureau
laws: Governed by the monastic community under Greek law; religious authority of the Ecumenical Patriarch
challenge: Continuing self-rule within Greece
recognition: Recognised as an autonomous region of Greece; UNESCO listed 1988
story: Mount Athos is a 335-square-kilometre peninsula in northern Greece holding 20 Orthodox monasteries. Monks have lived there since at least the 9th century. Most of the peninsula is run as an autonomous region of Greece by the monastic community, under the church authority of the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. A 10th-century charter bars female animals, and Greek law and religious tradition exclude women, who may not come within 500 metres of the coast. Dr Graham Speake, an author on Athos, told the BBC that women were not mentioned in the charter because everyone already knew they were not allowed in men's monasteries. Tradition also holds that the Virgin Mary was blown off course and landed there. To enter, a man sends a copy of his passport to the Pilgrims' Bureau. Each day 100 Orthodox and 10 non-Orthodox men are admitted for three nights. Vladimir Putin has visited to mark 1,000 years of Russian monks there. UNESCO listed the site in 1988. It stays part of the Greek state, with this special status.
mechanism: A religious community can keep real self-government and even an entry permit system for more than a thousand years by being recognised in the state's own law.

sources.t: Why are women banned from Mount Athos? (BBC)

name: Sovereign Military Order of Malta
founder: Blessed Gerard; recognised by Pope Paschal II
pop: Three principal officers count as citizens; no resident territory
laws: Constitution, Grand Master, treaties
challenge: Lost Malta to Napoleon in 1798 yet kept sovereign status
recognition: Diplomatic relations with 118 countries and the EU, by its own count; UN observer since 1994
story: The Order of Malta began in the 11th century as a hospital community in Jerusalem, and Pope Paschal II approved it in a bull of 15 February 1113. It later ruled Rhodes and then Malta, defending the latter for more than three months against the Ottomans in the Great Siege of 1565. In June 1798 Napoleon's forces took Malta, and the Order lost its last territory. It remains a sovereign subject of international law with no land, its only property being two headquarters buildings in Rome that have extraterritorial status, meaning Italian law treats them as outside normal Italian control. It issues its own passports, coins and stamps, and signs treaties. Its website reports diplomatic relations with 118 countries and the European Union, and cooperation agreements with over 50 states. Wikipedia gives 115 states. The UN General Assembly made it a permanent observer in 1994, citing its humanitarian work. Three principal officers count as citizens. Its diplomatic network, it says, exists to give its medical programmes protected access in crisis regions.
mechanism: Sovereignty in the sense of diplomatic recognition can survive complete loss of territory, if enough states keep treating the entity as a sovereign partner.

name: Vatican City and the Lateran Treaty
founder: Pope Pius XI and Benito Mussolini
laws: Papal rule; Holy See is itself a sovereign entity
challenge: Survived; revised by agreement in 1984
recognition: Recognised by Italy by treaty; treated as a sovereign state
story: The popes ruled the Papal States until Italian forces captured Rome in 1870. The Law of Guarantees of 1871 offered the pope use of the Vatican and Lateran palaces and 3,250,000 lire a year, but no sovereignty. The Holy See refused, and each pope after that called himself a prisoner in the Vatican. For about 60 years the dispute, called the Roman Question, stayed open. On 11 February 1929, at the Lateran Palace, the Holy See under Pius XI and Italy under Victor Emmanuel III and Mussolini signed the Lateran Pacts, and the Italian Parliament ratified them on 7 June. The treaty recognised full sovereignty of the Holy See over the newly created State of Vatican City, and a financial agreement settled claims over lost land. Italy's 1948 constitution recognised the treaty, and a 1984 revision ended Catholicism's status as the sole state religion.
