Vatican City covers 44 hectares, is an enclave in Rome, and had 882 residents in 2024. It is the smallest state in the world by both area and population.
mechanism: A new sovereign state can be created by a bilateral treaty with its host, and its legitimacy rests on the host's consent and wider diplomatic acceptance.

name: Liberstad
founder: Liberstad Drift AS, custodian; individual founders not confirmed
pop: 120 land buyers reported; no residents confirmed
currency: Cryptocurrency; bitcoin or Norwegian krone accepted for land
laws: Private contract rules; non-aggression principle
challenge: Not challenged; Norwegian law applies
recognition: None sought, by its own account
cost: Plots priced $9,400 to $47,100 for 1,000 to 5,000 square metres
story: Liberstad is a planned private city on three parcels totalling about 150 hectares in rural southern Norway, a few hours from Kristiansand, near the village of Bjelland. Its backers sold land from 2015, in bitcoin or Norwegian krone, at between about $9,400 for 1,000 square metres and $47,100 for 5,000 square metres. A company called Liberstad Drift AS was to hold the land records and act as custodian. The idea, based on the writing of Mises, Hayek and Rothbard, is to provide government services without a government, with minimal rules and no taxes. A 2017 Cointelegraph report said development would begin on 1 June if enough plots sold. The Startup Societies Foundation reported that 120 people had bought land and said the project does not demand sovereignty of any type, describing it as an experiment in how society could work. None of the pages retrieved for this record shows a finished settlement or a permanent population.
mechanism: A private land sale can create a voluntary community, but buying land in Norway does not remove it from Norwegian law or tax.

sources.t: Liberstad: A little piece of freedom in Norway (Startup Societies Foundation)
Bitcoin City Liberstad to begin development (Cointelegraph)

name: Praxis
challenge: Greenland idea rejected by a Danish MP; no site secured
cost: $525m reported: $500m conditional drawdown from GEM Digital plus $25m
story: Praxis is a New York company founded in 2019 by Dryden Brown, a former hedge fund analyst, and Charlie Callinan. That year they went to Nigeria and Ghana and proposed a financial centre to Ghana's vice-president. The firm later described plans for a city of 10,000 people, first in the Mediterranean, then in Greenland, then in Uruguay. In 2024 Gizmodo, citing the Wall Street Journal, reported $525 million in new funding. Of this, $500 million was a drawdown facility from the crypto firm GEM Digital, meaning money is released only after conditions are met, here listing Praxis tokens on a public exchange. In 2024 Brown wrote that he had flown to Nuuk to try to buy Greenland, then told TechCrunch he hoped instead to work with the government on a new city on uninhabitable land. Danish MP Rasmus Jarlov replied that Greenlandic independence needs Danish parliament approval and constitutional change. The pin on this map marks Nuuk, where Brown went, since Praxis has not announced a confirmed site. No city has been built.
mechanism: A would-be state with no land has only a financing plan; every candidate site still needs a host government to agree.

sources.t: I went to Greenland to try to buy it (TechCrunch)

name: Zuzalu
stopped_by: Ended as planned after about two months
laws: Community rules; no legal status
challenge: No challenge; a temporary gathering
story: Zuzalu was a pop-up city community conceived by Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin. It began on 25 March 2023 and ran for about two months at the resort of Lustica Bay on the Montenegrin coast, using hotels and rented homes. About 200 people from crypto, drug companies, politics and universities took part. Topics included cryptocurrency, AI, longevity science and the network state, an idea from former Coinbase executive Balaji Srinivasan in which an online community eventually buys land and seeks its own laws. He appeared by video. Decrypt described it as being compared by some to Burning Man for futurists and by others to a sleepaway camp for the crypto elite. The longevity group VitaDAO helped organise the science programme. No land was taken and the sources report no new law. People stayed in resort hotels and rented homes inside Montenegro, and went home at the end of the two months.
mechanism: A temporary gathering tests community-building with no need for land or sovereignty; it stayed fully within host-country law.

sources.t: Meet the Crypto Rich Who Want to Live Forever: Inside Zuzalu (Decrypt)

name: Forest City
pop: 9,000 according to the developer, against a target of 700,000
laws: Malaysian law; Special Financial Zone tax rules from 2025
challenge: Developer debts undermine it; no sovereignty challenge
story: Forest City is a US$100 billion housing project in Johor, Malaysia, about a 30-minute drive from Singapore, started in 2016 by the Chinese developer Country Garden. It was marketed mainly to mainland Chinese buyers as a luxury home for 700,000 people. Country Garden told Bloomberg that 9,000 people lived there, while Domus reported in July 2024 that just over 1 percent of the development was estimated to be inhabited. Business Insider reported the company had over US$190 billion in liabilities. On 20 September 2024 Malaysia launched a Special Financial Zone covering the area, with tax breaks from early 2025. They included a zero rate for family offices, private firms that run the wealth of rich families, and reduced personal income tax for some individuals who move there. Second Finance Minister Amir Hamzah Azizan spoke at the launch. Analysts quoted by BenarNews had mixed views on whether this would work. The project never sought sovereignty, and its special status is a state-backed tax arrangement.
mechanism: A state can create a special tax zone to rescue a private development; tax privileges come from the state and do not reduce its authority.

sources.t: Malaysia offers tax breaks to revive Forest City (BenarNews)
Forest City, the case of the ghost town (Domus)
Malaysia's $100 billion ghost town (Business Insider via Yahoo)

name: Akon City
stopped_by: Sapco, Senegal's state tourism development body, said in 2025 it no longer exists
challenge: Cancelled by a state agency that controlled the land deal
recognition: Backed by Senegal's government at first
story: In June 2018, at the Cannes Lions festival, the singer Akon, who was born in the United States and partly raised in Senegal, announced a crypto city that he said would run on his Akoin currency. He said President Macky Sall had given him 2,000 acres, about 800 hectares. On 13 January 2020 he signed a memorandum of understanding with Sapco, the state-owned tourism body, in the presence of the tourism minister. A groundbreaking ceremony followed in August 2020. The reported cost was $6 billion, to come mainly from American private partners, with a first phase by 2023 and completion by 2029. Commentators compared the curving tower designs with Wakanda from the Black Panther films. In 2025 the head of Sapco, Serigne Mamadou Mboup, told the BBC that the Akon City project no longer exists. He said Akon and Sapco had reached an agreement on a more realistic project that Sapco would support.
mechanism: A charter-style city still depends on a state agency's land allocation, which the state can withdraw if no building follows.

sources.t: The rise and fall of Akon City: a timeline (Ecofin Agency)

name: Bitcoin City
laws: Almost total tax exemption planned, with 13 percent value-added tax
challenge: Undercut by an IMF deal limiting the bitcoin policy
cost: US$1bn "volcano bond" planned; half for the city and half to buy bitcoin
story: In November 2021 El Salvador's president Nayib Bukele announced a city in La Union, at the foot of the Conchagua volcano, with geothermal power from the volcano used to mine bitcoin. The city was to be circular, like a coin. It would be almost free of taxes except for a 13 percent value-added tax, half of which would pay off bonds. Funding was to come from a US$1 billion volcano bond, involving the state power company LaGeo, with half the money for the city and half for buying bitcoin. Some bond buyers might receive Salvadoran citizenship. NBC reported that analysts paid more attention to the bonds than to the city, under a heading on desperation to seek financing. Delays in financing and construction followed. Under a later arrangement with the International Monetary Fund, businesses were freed from having to accept bitcoin, and taxes could no longer be paid in it. The Week described this as ending bitcoin's run as effective legal tender. The latest sources read for this record still describe the city as only planned.
mechanism: A government can promise a low-tax zone by decree, but its finances remain subject to lenders and bond markets, which can end the plan.

sources.t: El Salvador Bitcoin city planned at base of volcano (BBC)
The collapse of El Salvador's bitcoin dream (The Week)

name: Somaliland
founder: Somaliland authorities after the 10-year war against Siad Barre's government
laws: Elected governments since 1991
challenge: Survived 34 years without recognition; Somalia still claims it
recognition: Israel, 26 December 2025, the first and only UN member; offices of Ethiopia and Taiwan
story: Somaliland covers 176,120 square kilometres on the Gulf of Aden, with about 6.2 million people. It was a British protectorate that united with Somalia, but the constitution ratified in a 1961 referendum had little support in the north. Harsh policies against the Isaaq clan under Siad Barre led to a 10-year war, which ended with a declaration of independence in 1991 as Somalia descended into civil war. Since then Somaliland has held its own elections, run its own government and issued its own currency, the Somaliland shilling. The New York Times reported that it has governed most of the land it claims largely in peace and stability. Without recognition, it has informal ties and hosts offices from Ethiopia and Taiwan. On 26 December 2025 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu signed an agreement recognising it as an independent and sovereign state, the first UN member to do so. The Times notes other governments fear recognition could encourage other secessions.
mechanism: A place can meet the practical tests of statehood for decades (people, land, government, foreign contacts) and still lack recognition, which is a political decision by other states.

sources.t: Israel recognises Somaliland as independent state (The National)
Israel becomes the first nation to recognize Somaliland (NYT via Hawaii Tribune-Herald)

name: Transnistria
founder: Local leaders in Tiraspol, with Russian troops' support in 1992
passports: Own citizenship, unrecognised; most also hold Moldovan, many Russian, Romanian or Ukrainian
laws: Own government, parliament, military, police, central bank
challenge: Survived the 1992 war; status frozen
recognition: None by any UN member, not even Russia; other breakaway states only
story: Transnistria is a narrow strip east of the Dniester river, legally part of Moldova. On 2 September 1990 an ad hoc assembly proclaimed a separate Soviet republic there, amid fears that Moldova would reunite with Romania as the Soviet Union fell apart. A 1992 war killed about 1,000 people, and Russian troops already stationed there intervened on the separatists' side. The ceasefire has held, and the status remains unsettled. Transnistria runs its own government, parliament, army, police, post office and vehicle plates. Its central bank issues the Transnistrian ruble, which can be exchanged only inside the territory. Its population fell from 555,347 in 2004 to 475,373 in 2015. Many residents hold Moldovan citizenship, and many also hold Russian, Romanian or Ukrainian passports. Russia keeps soldiers there but, Deutsche Welle reports, does not recognise it as a state. A resident told DW he was arrested four times for disrespecting state order. On 4 September 2024 its parliament banned the term Transnistria in public, with a fine or up to 15 days in jail.
mechanism: Military backing can hold a de facto state in place for decades, and the citizens solve its non-recognition by carrying a recognised country's passport.

name: Taiwan
laws: Own constitution, elected government and courts
challenge: Survives; the People's Republic of China claims it
recognition: 11 UN members and the Holy See
story: Taiwan shows how recognition can limit a state that has everything else. The Republic of China controls Taiwan and nearby islands, 36,193 square kilometres with about 23.9 million people. It was a founding member of the United Nations, but in 1971 UN members voted to recognise the People's Republic of China as China's representative. The ROC kept claiming to be the sole government of all China until 1991, when it stopped treating the Communist Party as a rebel group and accepted its control of the mainland. The People's Republic claims Taiwan and refuses diplomatic relations with any country that recognises the ROC, so states have to choose. Taiwan now has formal relations with only 11 of the 193 UN members and the Holy See. Its foreign ministry lists them, among them Paraguay, Guatemala, Belize, Eswatini and Palau. Many others keep unofficial ties. It has territory, a population and an effective government, and few states deal with it formally.
mechanism: Effective government and a large population do not ensure recognition, because recognition is decided by other states weighing a rival claimant.

sources.t: Diplomatic Allies (Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Republic of China)

name: Orania
laws: Application-based entry; last transitional representative council in South Africa
challenge: Not challenged directly; South African government opposes the idea but has generally ignored it
story: Orania is a town on the Orange River in the Northern Cape of South Africa. In 1990, in the last years of apartheid, Carel Boshoff III, a son-in-law of apartheid architect Hendrik Verwoerd, and a number of families bought an abandoned workers' village. He hoped that hundreds of thousands of Afrikaners would one day live there, in a state of their own, called a Volkstaat. In 2016 CNN reported about 1,300 residents. To live there, a person must apply and be accepted as an Afrikaner, speak Afrikaans, have a clean criminal record, and share the group's goals. CNN and other outside observers describe the town as whites-only, an account the community disputes. It prints its own money-like coupons for use in its stores, and it keeps the last transitional representative council in the country, a local-government form from the end of apartheid. The South African government has said it opposes a whites-only community but has generally ignored the town. After Boshoff died in 2011, his son took over the Orania Movement.
mechanism: Private purchase and a selective membership process can create a near-separate community under national law, raising a conflict with the state's equality principles that it has chosen not to force.

sources.t: Inside Orania, South Africa's whites-only town (CNN)

name: Zapatista autonomous territories
laws: Councils of Good Government to 2023; since then Local Autonomous Governments
challenge: Survives after 1994 uprising; relations with the state remain strained
story: On 1 January 1994, the day the North American Free Trade Agreement began, masked Mayan farmers of the Zapatista Army of National Liberation briefly seized several cities in Chiapas, one of Mexico's poorest states. Their name honours Emiliano Zapata, a hero of the 1910 revolution. The fighting stopped, and they kept control of their own communities. From 1994 to 2003 the territories were organised around community centres called Aguascalientes. In 2003 these were replaced by Caracoles, regional centres, with autonomous municipalities run by Councils of Good Government. Al Jazeera reported from Oventic in 2014 that the Zapatistas had established complete political and economic autonomy, and that they governed and policed their own communities across five regions. It also reported that relations with the state stayed strained. In 2023, after increased cartel violence, the EZLN announced that the autonomous municipalities would dissolve and be replaced by Local Autonomous Governments, grouped in collectives and regional assemblies. No state recognises this as a separate country, and the Zapatistas operate inside Mexico.
mechanism: A rural movement backed by armed force can hold real self-government for decades without formal status, by ruling over its own people and avoiding formal secession.

sources.t: Are Mexico's Zapatista rebels still relevant? (Al Jazeera)

name: Republic of Texas movement
stopped_by: Texas law enforcement and courts
pop: Followers at a compound in the Davis Mountains; claims of 40,000 supporters statewide
laws: Claimed a provisional government
challenge: Failed: leaders jailed after a week-long standoff
story: The Republic of Texas is a movement, started by Richard Lance McLaren, that says the 1845 annexation of Texas was illegal and that the state remains an independent nation under occupation. It claims to have reinstated a provisional government on 13 December 1995. McLaren argued that Texas is a captive nation of war in international law, a claim scholars do not support. The movement split into three factions in 1996, and activists claim more than 40,000 supporters. In 1997 McLaren and followers kidnapped Joe and Margaret Ann Rowe, held them hostage at the Davis Mountain Resort, and demanded the release of a member in exchange. After a week-long standoff with police and Texas Rangers, McLaren's wife Evelyn convinced him to give up. He and four others went to prison. Two other members, Richard Keyes III and Mike Matson, slipped away at first. In June 1998 Keyes was convicted of burglary with intent to commit aggravated assault and sentenced to 90 years.
mechanism: When a legal theory of secession turns to hostage-taking, ordinary criminal law decides the outcome and the theory never reaches any court as a sovereignty question.

name: Republic of Artsakh
stopped_by: Azerbaijan's military offensive of 2023
laws: Own president, parliament, elections
challenge: Defeated by force after 32 years
recognition: None; its elections were rejected by the EU, US and others
story: Artsakh, also called Nagorno-Karabakh, was a breakaway state inside the borders of Azerbaijan, with its capital at Stepanakert. From 1991 it controlled parts of the former Soviet autonomous region of Nagorno-Karabakh, and had its own president, parliament and elections. No UN member recognised it, and the European Union, the United States and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation rejected its elections as a source of tension. After the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war its territory shrank and it was left as an enclave within Azerbaijan, linked to Armenia by the Lachin corridor. In the 2023 offensive the Azerbaijani military took control of the land Artsakh still held, and the entire population was effectively expelled. On 28 September 2023 President Samvel Shahramanyan signed a decree dissolving all state institutions by 1 January 2024, although he later attempted to annul it.
mechanism: Without recognition, a de facto state has no international protection, and the state holding recognised title may recover it by force.

name: Achzivland
stopped_by: Founder died in 2018; Israel never recognised it
laws: One-man rule by "President" Avivi
challenge: Survived several attempts to remove him
story: Eli Avivi came across the site of Achziv on the northern Israeli coast near Lebanon in 1952, and he settled among the old buildings, selling fish to a nearby kibbutz. He later married Rina. In the 1960s the state decided to turn the area into a national park and sent bulldozers. Rina told the BBC that the army let him stay on condition that he worked as an undercover agent for the domestic intelligence agency, Shin Bet. When authorities put up a fence that blocked the couple's way to the sea, they tore up their passports in protest and declared independence in 1971. Achzivland had its own passport asking bearers be allowed to pass freely. It drew hippies and celebrities, including Sophia Loren. In 2015 the BBC reported that Avivi, then 85 and frail, said the state did everything it could to get him out. Israel never recognised the place. He died in May 2018, aged 88, leaving Rina, 71, as the only other citizen.
mechanism: A long-tolerated occupant may outlast the state's plans in a personal stand-off, but his personal status does not pass on as sovereignty.

sources.t: Achzivland: The tiny state inside Israel (BBC)

name: Republic of Whangamomona
laws: President chosen by vote on Republic Day
challenge: No challenge reported; a festival
story: Whangamomona is a small settlement in the interior of New Zealand's North Island. Its statistical area covers about 690 square kilometres and had 159 people at the 2023 census. In local government reforms in 1989 it was placed in the Manawatu-Wanganui Region, on the grounds that the Whangamomona River flows into the Whanganui River. Residents wanted to be in the Taranaki Region instead. On 1 November 1989, at what they called the first Republic Day, they responded by declaring themselves the Republic of Whangamomona. The declaration began as a pointed protest, and the town kept up the event as a yearly celebration, with a vote for president. It became a local festival that attracts visitors from across the North Island. In 2001 it moved to every two years, held in January to get better summer weather. The record here does not show any formal response by the New Zealand government. The dispute was about which regional council would govern the town, and the republic continues as a piece of local identity.
mechanism: An argument over an administrative boundary can become a lasting local identity, with the national legal order unaffected.

name: Principality of Wy
laws: Royal titles; arts patronage
challenge: Lost: failed in court appeal in 2013
story: The Principality of Wy is a house in the Sydney suburb of Mosman. In 1993 the Delprat family applied to build a driveway across an unbuilt road to reach their house, which started a long fight with Mosman Council. On 15 November 2004 the artist Paul Delprat declared that he had seceded from Mosman, though not from Australia, and named himself Prince. After 20 years seeking planning permission, he lost his appeal in 2013. Sky News, the Daily Telegraph in London, the Sydney Morning Herald, The National of Abu Dhabi and the Kuwait Times have all covered it, and it still has no local, national or international recognition. Delprat attended the first Australian conference of micronation leaders, held on Dangar Island in 2010 with sponsorship from Macquarie University. The community supports the arts and sponsors an art prize. Its claim is unusual in being aimed at a local council and leaving Australia's status untouched, and the outcome was decided by ordinary planning law, with the family failing to secure the driveway.
mechanism: Declaring secession from a council has no effect on planning law; the council's decision was tested and upheld through ordinary appeal.

name: Occupation of Alcatraz
founder: Richard Oakes and Indian students and urban activists
stopped_by: Armed federal marshals, FBI agents and special forces police on 10 June 1971
laws: Community governance by many tribes
challenge: Failed: removed after 19 months
story: Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay had held Indian prisoners, including 19 Hopi in January 1895. The General Services Administration, the US property agency, took charge of the site, and San Francisco wanted a park there. A brief occupation on 9 March 1964 raised the idea of a cultural centre and an Indian university. Richard Oakes, Indian students and urban Indians from the Bay Area planned a new landing on 9 November 1969. On 20 November that became a full occupation that lasted 19 months. The government cut off all electric power and removed the water barge that supplied fresh water. President Nixon approved a removal plan, to happen when there were the fewest people on the island and to use as little force as possible. On 10 June 1971 armed federal marshals, FBI agents and special forces police landed and removed five women, four children and six unarmed men. The National Park Service, which now runs the island, publishes this account.
mechanism: A symbolic claim to federal surplus land, grounded in treaty ideas, had no standing, and the government ended it by cutting off utilities and using federal police.

sources.t: We Hold the Rock (National Park Service)

name: Capitol Hill Occupied Protest
founder: Protesters after the murder of George Floyd
stopped_by: Seattle police, 1 July 2020
challenge: Cleared by police after 23 days
story: In May 2020 a police officer in Minneapolis murdered George Floyd. Tense confrontations between protesters and riot police began in Seattle's Capitol Hill neighbourhood on 1 June 2020. On 8 June protesters set up a self-declared autonomous zone, at first named Free Capitol Hill and later the Capitol Hill Autonomous Zone, or CHAZ, then the Capitol Hill Occupied Protest, or CHOP. It covered two intersections at the corners of Cal Anderson Park and the roads leading up to them. Police cleared the area on 1 July 2020, after 23 days. It is included here as the shortest case on this list and as a test of what happens when a zone forms in the middle of a large US city. The zone made no claim to be a country and sought no recognition. There is no sign in the page reviewed for this record that any court or government ever treated it as having any legal status beyond an occupation of public streets.
mechanism: Self-declared autonomy in a city centre has no legal effect, and it lasts only until local government chooses to send police.

name: ZAD de Notre-Dame-des-Landes
stopped_by: French state evictions in 2018; remaining projects then took legal status
laws: Self-organised communal structures
challenge: Blocked an airport; partly evicted, partly legalised
recognition: French government accepted some projects after 2018
story: Notre-Dame-des-Landes is a farming area of 1,650 hectares near Nantes in France. The state planned an airport there from the 1960s, and local farmers and environmental groups fought it for decades. In the 2000s much of the land was occupied by squatters, with farmers refusing to leave. The occupiers named it a Zone to Defend, or ZAD, and set up self-sufficient structures including a communal bakery and livestock farming. Attempts to clear the area met large public mobilisations in 2012 and 2018. In January 2018 President Emmanuel Macron announced that the airport would be shelved and that the existing Nantes airport would be redeveloped instead. Many of the remaining projects then entered a process of legalisation, moving from occupation into ordinary French land and farm law. The result differs from most entries on this map, since the occupiers succeeded in stopping the state's project on the ground that started the conflict. Their self-rule ended up as a set of negotiated permissions. The start year in this record is approximate.
mechanism: Prolonged occupation can stop a state project and win a negotiated right to stay, with the price being legal status under the same state.

name: Republic of Vevcani
passports: Issued as part of a tourism project
laws: Mock government
challenge: No state response reported; a tourist tradition by 2002
story: Vevcani is a village of about 2,400 people near Lake Ohrid in North Macedonia. BBC Travel reports that it has tried to declare independence three times from two countries in five decades. In 1987 it first threatened to secede from Yugoslavia. In 1991 it proclaimed itself an independent republic 11 days after the Yugoslav republic of Macedonia declared its own independence during the break-up of Yugoslavia. In 2002 locals revived the idea in a tongue-in-cheek way, to draw tourists and poke fun at politics, by flying a national flag, issuing passports and printing money. The village's springs are at the heart of its customs and celebrations. A local guide told the BBC that they are the most important part of its culture and history. The village also has its own customs at the springs, and these are promoted to visitors. North Macedonia has continued to govern the village as part of its territory.
mechanism: A secession bid made while a federation breaks up can turn into a harmless tourist brand once the new national state is firmly in place.

name: Republic of Le Saugeais
founder: Georges Pourchet, named by Louis Ottaviani
laws: President, prime minister, secretary-general, two customs officers, ambassadors
challenge: No challenge reported
story: Le Saugeais is a wooded valley in the Haut-Doubs in eastern France, along the Swiss border. In 1947 a senior official, Louis Ottaviani, leader of the Doubs region, stopped for lunch at a restaurant by the abbey in Montbenoit. The owner, Georges Pourchet, joked and asked if he had a permit to enter the territory of Le Saugeais. Ottaviani, enjoying the joke, said a place like that sounded like a republic, a republic needs a president, and named him President. The joke could have ended there. In May 1972 the abbey's priest and the mayor told Georgette's mother, Gabrielle, that the citizens wanted her to take over. A flag based on the old colours of Franche-Comte came in 1981, and a postal stamp in 1987. Georgette Bertin-Pourchet later became president after being unanimously elected. The government has a prime minister, a secretary-general, two customs officers and ambassadors. BBC Travel reports that her sitting room clock plays the national anthem, and the French state does not recognise the republic.
mechanism: A joke started by a state official has no legal effect, showing that a local identity can last 70 years without touching national law.

sources.t: A tiny country between France and Switzerland (BBC Travel)

name: Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria
founder: Kurdish-led forces and councils in the Syrian civil war
stopped_by: Syrian government offensive of January 2026 and an integration agreement
laws: Self-governing sub-regions
challenge: Lost territory to Turkey and to Syria; integrated on 20 August 2026
recognition: Not recognised by Syria or any state; recognised by the Parliament of Catalonia
story: During the Syrian civil war, in 2012, Kurdish-led forces took de facto control of parts of north-eastern Syria. The region later became the Democratic Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria, also known as Rojava. In March 2016 a federal system was announced, and Al Jazeera reported that it was declared by Kurdish groups. At various times it included the sub-regions of Afrin, Jazira, Euphrates, Raqqa, Tabqa, Manbij and Deir ez-Zor. It ran some foreign relations but was not recognised as autonomous by Syria or by any other state, although the Parliament of Catalonia recognised it. From 2016 Turkish forces and Turkish-backed Syrian rebels occupied parts of northern Syria in a series of operations. In January 2026 the Syrian transitional government took back those areas and launched an offensive in the north-east, capturing up to 80 percent of the administration's land, which was then ceded under an integration agreement. The administration fully joined the Syrian state on 20 August 2026. It lasted 14 years. The record here does not include current population figures.
mechanism: Self-rule won in a civil war lasts only while the central state is weak and foreign backers stay, and it can be folded back by a negotiated merger.

name: Northern Cyprus
founder: Turkish Cypriot leaders with Turkish support
laws: Own government; depends on Turkey
challenge: Survives under Turkish protection; UN declared the secession invalid
story: Northern Cyprus covers the northern third of the island of Cyprus, from Cape Apostolos Andreas in the north-east to Morphou Bay in the north-west. In 1974 a coup backed by the Greek military junta, seeking to annex the island, prompted Turkey to invade and capture the north. Much of the Greek Cypriot population in the north was evicted, and Turkish Cypriots fled from the south. In 1983 the Turkish-held north declared independence unilaterally, meaning without any agreement from the Republic of Cyprus. UN Security Council Resolution 541 rejected the declaration as legally invalid and urged UN members not to recognise it. Only Turkey does so, and the international community treats the area as Republic of Cyprus territory under Turkish military occupation. Attempts to settle the division have failed. Northern Cyprus relies on Turkey for economic, political and military support, leading some experts to call it a puppet state, while others dispute that description because of its separate politics.
mechanism: A Security Council call for non-recognition can keep a territory out of the international system for decades, while one patron state keeps it running in practice.

name: Wa State
founder: United Wa State Party, after breaking with the Communist Party of Burma
laws: Own political system, administrative divisions and army
challenge: Peace deal with Myanmar since 1989
recognition: Recognises Myanmar's sovereignty; part recognised in Myanmar's 2008 constitution as a self-administered area
story: Wa State is a self-governing region in Myanmar's Shan State, on the Chinese border. In 1989 Wa fighters split from the Communist Party of Burma and struck a peace deal with the central government. In return for stopping fighting, they were given land to run as they wished. They grew poppies, and the region became one of the world's leading producers of opium and heroin in the following decade. The ruling United Wa State Party has its own political system, administrative divisions and army. It accepts Myanmar's sovereignty over its territory but not allegiance to any specific government, and Myanmar's 2008 constitution recognises the northern part as a self-administered area. The BBC's Jonah Fisher visited in 2016 and reported that Google Maps does not show it and that visa requests were refused. The money is the Chinese yuan, the main language is Mandarin, and electricity and mobile networks come from Chinese companies. He said the region had schools and infrastructure, partly built with illicit money. An official told him visitors were assumed to be spies.
mechanism: An armed group can trade the claim of independence for near-total autonomy under a peace deal, relying on a neighbouring economy for money and services.

sources.t: Wa State: Inside Myanmar's secret state (BBC)

name: Cheran
founder: Women of Cheran, in the Purepecha town
laws: Council elected by four districts; political parties banned; community militia
challenge: Survived; treated as a self-ruling indigenous community
recognition: Treated as a self-ruling indigenous community
story: Cheran is a town of the Indigenous Purepecha people in Michoacan, Mexico. For more than three years, armed loggers and masked men demanding extortion had worked with impunity, and by 2011 the loggers were close to one of the town's water springs. A group of local women met in secret and decided to stop the trucks in town, where neighbours could back them up. The uprising drove out loggers, police and politicians. Political parties were banned and remained banned when the BBC visited five years later. Each of the town's four districts elected representatives to a ruling council. Armed checkpoints went up on the three main roads, staffed by the Ronda Comunitaria, a local force of men and women who stop every vehicle and question its occupants. The BBC described this as a return to older ways of governing, independent of outsiders. Sources describe the area today as a self-ruling Indigenous community largely free of the crime and corruption that caused the revolt. Cheran does not claim to be a separate country.
mechanism: An Indigenous community can replace state police and party politics inside its boundaries without seeking independence, showing a working route of local self-rule.

sources.t: Cheran: The town that threw out police, politicians and gangsters (BBC)
